rule: Debounce all interactive triggers to prevent double submissions from rapid tapping.
do_this: Debounce tap handlers or immediately disable interactive elements upon first trigger until the asynchronous action resolves
dont_do_this: Allow rapid successive taps to fire duplicate network requests or trigger redundant actions
trigger_context: Any primary action button or interactive element that triggers a mutation or network request
why: Rapid double-tapping causes duplicate transactions, double data saves, and severe user frustration.
example: Before: Button fires purchase API on every click. After: Button enters loading state and disables on first click.

rule: Display human-readable toast notifications for errors instead of raw system output.
do_this: Display contextual toast notifications or inline banners containing human-readable error messages
dont_do_this: Expose raw database exceptions, stack traces, or variable values like undefined directly to the UI
trigger_context: Any component handling API errors, network failures, or validation exceptions
why: Raw technical errors confuse users, break visual polish, and erode trust in the application stability.
example: Before: Screen displays 'TypeError: undefined is not a function'. After: Toast displays 'Unable to save changes. Please try again.'

rule: Pad or scroll viewports dynamically so the virtual keyboard never obscures active input fields.
do_this: Adjust container padding or scroll the active input into view dynamically when the software keyboard appears
dont_do_this: Let the software keyboard obscure the active input field entirely
trigger_context: Form inputs, textareas, and chat inputs positioned near the bottom of mobile viewports
why: Obscuring the input field prevents users from seeing what they are typing, leading to input abandonment.
example: Before: Bottom input field is hidden beneath the OS keyboard. After: Form scrolls up automatically to keep the focused input visible.

rule: Verify accessible contrast ratios for all elements across both light and dark theme toggles.
do_this: Audit all token values across both dark and light modes to maintain WCAG compliant contrast ratios in every state
dont_do_this: Hardcode color values or rely on inversion algorithms that result in unreadable low-contrast text
trigger_context: UI components, text, and icons that dynamically switch between dark and light themes
why: Unverified theme switching causes text to blend into backgrounds, rendering the interface completely unreadable.
example: Before: Gray text remains dark gray when switching to dark mode, disappearing into the background. After: Text tokens dynamically switch to light gray for high contrast.

rule: Persist form input state locally so user entries are preserved when navigating backward.
do_this: Persist user input state in local storage, route state, or form management stores across navigation events
dont_do_this: Clear input values or unmount state when a user hits the back button
trigger_context: Multi-step workflows, forms, and input screens where a user might navigate backward
why: Losing typed data upon hitting the back button destroys user effort and causes extreme friction.
example: Before: Hitting back clears all entered form fields. After: Returning to the form restores previously typed inputs from state cache.

rule: Avoid generic dark slate and centered purple blur hero backgrounds in favor of unique brand-aligned surface treatments.
do_this: Utilize bespoke, context-driven surface treatments, custom brand palette pairings, or subtle mesh gradients instead of defaulting to a dark slate background with a centered generic purple radial blur.
dont_do_this: Default to Tailwind slate-900 combined with a centralized, blurred purple radial gradient orb.
trigger_context: The primary landing page hero section background layer
why: Relying on default AI-generated background aesthetics immediately signals uninspired template creation, eroding user trust before they read the value proposition.
example: Before: Slate-900 canvas with an obnoxious fuchsia center blob. After: Deep charcoal textured surface paired with subtle, asymmetric contextual illumination.

rule: Eliminate redundant rounded square icon containers for feature bullet points.
do_this: Pair standalone icons directly with typography, use minimalist inline indicators, or design purpose-built structured containers that match the exact visual weight of the accompanying text.
dont_do_this: Enclose every single feature list icon inside an identical, generic rounded square background badge.
trigger_context: Feature checklist or benefit bullet-point lists utilizing icons
why: Enclosing every single icon in an identical container creates visual noise and repetitive chunking that reduces scannability.
example: Before: Every bullet point features a standalone icon inside a rounded grey container box. After: Clean typographic hierarchy with minimal inline vector glyphs.

rule: Avoid arbitrary height inflation and glowing borders for featured pricing cards.
do_this: Establish emphasis through thoughtful hierarchy, explicit value propositions, clean typography, and restrained badge placement rather than arbitrary dimensional scaling and glowing outlines.
dont_do_this: Scale the featured pricing card to be precisely 10 pixels taller and wrap it in an artificial glowing border.
trigger_context: Multi-tier product pricing matrix components
why: Literal height offsets and glowing borders look gimmicky and distract from evaluating actual plan features and pricing metrics.
example: Before: Middle pricing card scaled up +10px with a neon border. After: Subtle shadow elevation, distinct surface tint, and a clean 'Recommended' badge.

rule: Ensure every cell in a bento grid contains genuine, informative product data rather than empty decorative animations.
do_this: Populate grid cells with authentic product data, real-time metrics, actual code snippets, or functional UI widgets.
dont_do_this: Construct empty bento grid cards containing purely decorative static CSS charts and pointless bouncing toggles.
trigger_context: Marketing bento grid layouts and feature showcases
why: Empty placeholder metrics and looping mock animations degrade user confidence by exposing a lack of substantive product depth.
example: Before: Bento card with a static bar chart and an idle looping toggle. After: Bento card showing live API latency metrics and functional telemetry graphs.

rule: Keep UI preview mockups flat or subtly angled, avoiding extreme 3D perspectives with heavy blur shadows.
do_this: Render product interfaces flat or at clean, readable isometric angles with soft, physically plausible ambient drop shadows.
dont_do_this: Tilt dashboard preview mockups at an extreme 15-degree 3D perspective paired with heavy 40-pixel blurred drop shadows.
trigger_context: Hero dashboard previews and application UI mockups
why: Exaggerated perspective distortion sacrifices legibility of the actual interface content just for cheap visual flair.
example: Before: Dashboard preview skewed at a steep 15-degree angle with a blown-out dark drop shadow. After: Clean, front-facing UI shot with crisp edge rendering.

rule: Always implement content-matching skeleton loaders instead of spinners to improve perceived loading speed.
do_this: Replace generic spinning loaders with structural skeleton loaders that mirror the layout and dimensions of the incoming content.
dont_do_this: Use generic spinning indicators or blank white screens for predictable layout content fetches.
trigger_context: Any asynchronous content fetching or data-loading screen state
why: Spinners create a sense of stalling and disconnect user focus, whereas structural skeletons provide a spatial preview that tricks the brain into perceiving faster load times.
example: Before: Centered spinner icon. After: Gray pulsing placeholder blocks matching cards and text lines.

principle: Instant Touch Feedback and Optimistic UI
rule: Provide immediate visual state changes upon tap interaction and handle heavy processing asynchronously in the background.
do_this: Acknowledge every user tap immediately with visual state changes, executing heavy processes asynchronously in the background.
dont_do_this: Leave the UI frozen or unresponsive during network latency while waiting for server confirmation.
trigger_context: Any interactive button or touch target that fires a network request or heavy background task
why: Unresponsive interfaces break the illusion of direct manipulation and make the application feel broken or sluggish.
example: Before: Button hangs with no state change for 3 seconds during upload. After: Button instantly transitions to a loading/success state while the upload runs asynchronously.

principle: Consistent Primary Action Placement in Flows
rule: Maintain absolute positional consistency for primary action buttons throughout multi-step sequences.
do_this: Anchor the primary continue or advance action button to the exact same screen coordinate across every step of the flow.
dont_do_this: Shift primary action buttons to different vertical or horizontal positions between sequential screens.
trigger_context: Multi-step onboarding flows, checkout wizards, or sequential form screens
why: Shifting buttons forces users to visually hunt for the target on every step, breaking muscle memory and increasing cognitive load.
example: Before: Continue button is at the bottom in step one and in the middle in step two. After: Continue button remains pinned to the bottom-fixed action bar across all steps.

principle: Complete Application Edge States and Flows
rule: Design dedicated UI views for empty data collections, active loading skeletons, and runtime error handlers for every functional screen.
do_this: Implement explicit UI screens and feedback mechanisms for asynchronous data fetching, data-absent conditions, and failure states before considering a product finished.
dont_do_this: Assume an interface is complete when happy-path layouts function correctly without handling empty, loading, and error states.
trigger_context: Any application pre-launch checklist or production readiness audit for a new software interface.
why: Failing to account for non-ideal states results in broken layouts, blank screens, and user confusion when network latency or empty databases occur.
example: Before: A dashboard displaying blank white space when no data exists. After: An empty state component featuring custom illustration, explanatory microcopy, and a clear call-to-action button to create the first item.

principle: Avoid Overused AI-Generated UI Tropes and Generic Layout Patterns
rule: Eliminate unoriginal template aesthetics and generic boilerplate interface components that signal low-effort automated generation.
do_this: design bespoke layouts with purpose-driven typography, authentic content, and restrained visual styling tailored to the specific product identity
dont_do_this: rely on cliché AI styling tropes such as default bento grids, liquid glass effects, random sparkle icons, neon-on-dark palettes, and generic three-tier pricing cards without actual product differentiation
trigger_context: marketing landing pages, feature grids, and pricing sections generated via AI tools
why: Overused aesthetic tropes create visual fatigue, reduce brand trust, and make interfaces look indistinguishable from low-effort automated clones.
example: Before: A dark mode landing page featuring purple glow effects, floating dot grids, terminal windows, and floating checkmark bullets. After: A clean, content-first layout with high-contrast neutral typography and contextual product screenshots.

rule: Ensure all layout containers fit strictly within the mobile viewport width to completely prevent horizontal scrolling.
do_this: Audit and eliminate any elements or layout containers that extend horizontally beyond the primary viewport boundary.
dont_do_this: Allow wide content blocks, unconstrained images, or fixed-width containers to force horizontal scrolling on mobile viewports.
trigger_context: Responsive web layouts viewed on mobile devices with constrained viewport widths
why: Horizontal scrolling on mobile creates a broken, jarring user experience and indicates layout containment failure.
example: Before: A fixed-width data table causing horizontal page panning. After: A responsive container with CSS overflow handling or stacked mobile representation.

rule: Convert all visible phone numbers and email addresses into functional interactive links.
do_this: Wrap phone numbers in 'tel:' anchors and email addresses in 'mailto:' anchors with clear interactive affordances.
dont_do_this: Render phone numbers and email addresses as static, unlinked plain text.
trigger_context: Phone numbers and email addresses displayed in headers, footers, or contact sections
why: Users on mobile devices expect touch targets to immediately initiate phone calls or open their default email client.
example: Before: Plain text string '+1 (555) 019-2834'. After: An interactive anchor tag `+1 (555) 019-2834`.

rule: Display clear, contextual success and error message components upon form interaction.
do_this: Provide immediate, visually distinct success messages upon completion and explicit error messages for failed submissions.
dont_do_this: Leave the interface completely static or silent after a user submits a form, causing uncertainty.
trigger_context: Interactive forms, newsletter signups, or contact modals handling user submissions
why: Users require explicit system feedback to confirm whether their action was successfully processed or requires correction.
example: Before: Form clears silently on submit with no confirmation. After: Form renders an inline green success banner stating 'Message sent successfully!'.

rule: Ensure subscription cancellation flows require no more steps or clicks than the original sign-up process.
do_this: Provide a direct, single-action cancellation path that requires equal or fewer interaction steps than the initial subscription onboarding flow.
dont_do_this: Bury the cancellation trigger behind multi-step confirmation screens, deceptive dark patterns, retention questionnaires, or hidden navigation paths.
trigger_context: Account settings, billing dashboards, or subscription management interfaces where users attempt to downgrade or terminate a paid plan.
why: Making cancellation unnecessarily arduous creates cognitive friction and violates consumer protection standards, leading to severe legal penalties and severe brand erosion.
example: Before: Requiring a 5-step retention survey, chat with support, and two confirmation pages to cancel. After: A single 'Cancel Subscription' button in billing settings that processes immediately with one confirmation dialog.

rule: Discard any input source lacking concrete UI/UX design mechanics, layout values, component states, or accessibility directives.
do_this: Filter out promotional creator metadata, personal branding hooks, and off-topic social captions that contain no interface design instructions.
dont_do_this: Process non-design text, general marketing copy, or personal introduction statements through design rule extraction engines.
trigger_context: Any unstructured content intake or social media corpus ingestion pipeline
why: Ingesting non-design content contaminates design system guidelines with irrelevant noise, reducing the precision and reliability of the synthesized skill set.
example: Before: Extracting principles from a general bio. After: Returning an empty array `[]` when no design context is present.

rule: Audit and correct all color contrast pairs to satisfy WCAG accessibility standards across the entire application interface
do_this: Verify and adjust all text-to-background color combinations to meet or exceed WCAG minimum contrast ratio thresholds
dont_do_this: Deploy low-contrast color pairings that cause readability strain for users with visual impairments
trigger_context: Any web page or UI component containing text displayed over background surfaces
why: Insufficient contrast makes text unreadable for users with low vision or when viewing displays under high ambient lighting, causing abandonment.
example: Before: Light gray text on a white background (#CCCCCC on #FFFFFF). After: Dark slate text on a white background (#333333 on #FFFFFF).

rule: Limit the interface to one singular high-contrast color for the primary call-to-action element
do_this: Designate a single, highly distinct accent color dedicated exclusively to the primary conversion action on the screen
dont_do_this: Use multiple competing saturated colors for primary actions, which dilutes visual hierarchy and user focus
trigger_context: Landing pages, conversion funnels, and primary interaction screens
why: Multiple competing primary colors create cognitive load and paralyze decision-making, lowering conversion rates.
example: Before: Multiple vibrant blue and orange buttons in the hero section. After: One prominent emerald green primary button with secondary actions styled as ghost buttons.

rule: Use spring-based physics curves and platform-native transition patterns for all interactive state changes and sheet presentations.
do_this: Implement physics-based spring animations and match OS-native navigation transitions while respecting user reduced-motion accessibility preferences
dont_do_this: Use generic, web-style linear or ease-in-out easing curves that feel disconnected from the platform's native feel
trigger_context: interactive touch targets, modal sheets, and page transitions in mobile applications
why: Web-styled motion feels sluggish and unpolished on native hardware, violating user expectations for fluid, tactile feedback and causing cognitive friction.
example: Before: A modal slides up using a standard linear ease. After: A modal uses a damped spring animation that responds to a swipe-to-dismiss gesture with matching velocity.

rule: Provide a high-resolution preview image and standard metadata tags for all shared product links.
do_this: Define explicit OpenGraph and Twitter card image metadata tags accompanied by a descriptive title and subtitle so shared links render a rich visual card instead of a generic placeholder frame.
dont_do_this: Leave link metadata unconfigured, resulting in a fallback blank grey box or missing thumbnail when users share the application URL.
trigger_context: any web application URL or product link shared across social media or messaging platforms
why: Missing link previews diminish perceived professional quality and reduce click-through rates on external platforms.
example: Adding og:image, og:title, and twitter:image tags to the document head of the landing page.

rule: Direct first-time users to a singular primary action explaining the application value within the initial screen.
do_this: Guide the user directly to a single, high-value primary action that immediately demonstrates the core utility of the application.
dont_do_this: Drop unguided new users into an empty state or generic dashboard without clear direction toward the primary value proposition.
trigger_context: first-time user authentication and post-signup application entry flows
why: Unguided initial states cause high abandonment rates because users fail to discover the core product utility.
example: Presenting a prominent prompt to create a first project instantly upon logging in rather than showing a blank dashboard.

rule: Always place the primary call-to-action above the fold to ensure immediate user engagement upon viewport load.
do_this: Position the primary conversion trigger or call-to-action within the initial viewport before any vertical scrolling is required.
dont_do_this: Bury the primary conversion action below secondary content blocks or deep down the page layout.
trigger_context: Any landing page, marketing site, or conversion-focused web view viewport initialization.
why: Users evaluate page value within seconds of arrival; hiding primary actions below the fold drastically increases bounce rates and reduces conversion velocity.
example: Hero section featuring a prominent primary 'Get Started' button visible immediately without scrolling versus a hero section showing only text where the button sits far down.

rule: Fix the primary conversion action to the bottom of mobile viewports as a sticky element during scroll.
do_this: Implement a pinned or sticky bottom action bar containing the primary conversion trigger on mobile viewports.
dont_do_this: Force mobile users to scroll back to the top of long-form pages or hunt through navigation menus to complete a conversion action.
trigger_context: Mobile web layouts and responsive viewports where vertical scrolling spans multiple content sections.
why: Mobile viewports have restricted vertical space; keeping the conversion trigger persistently accessible reduces interaction cost and friction.
example: A sticky bottom bar featuring a 'Buy Now' button that remains anchored while scrolling through product details.

rule: Display explicit loading states for every async data fetch or user action to prevent perceived unresponsiveness.
do_this: Provide dedicated visual indicators, skeleton screens, or spinners for all pending asynchronous actions and data loads.
dont_do_this: Leave the interface completely static and unresponsive while network requests or background data fetches are processing.
trigger_context: Any interface component, button, or container that fetches asynchronous data or submits a network request.
why: Without visual feedback during latency spikes, users assume the system froze and will repeatedly tap or abandon the interface.
example: Transforming a button into a spinner state immediately upon tap while network requests resolve.

principle: Inline Form Validation and Error States
rule: Provide clear, contextual error states and inline validation messages for every form input failure.
do_this: Design explicit, contextual error states with clear recovery instructions directly adjacent to invalid form fields.
dont_do_this: Rely solely on generic, unhelpful system alerts or leave fields unstyled when validation fails.
trigger_context: Any user input form, multi-step checkout flow, or interactive data submission interface.
why: Vague or absent error states cause user confusion, form abandonment, and high cognitive load during data entry.
example: Highlighting an invalid email input field with a distinct red border and explanatory text reading 'Please enter a valid email format' below it.

rule: Complete all primary interface interactions within 400 milliseconds.
do_this: Execute state updates and feedback animations within a 400-millisecond window to ensure perceived system instantaneousness.
dont_do_this: Allow interaction response times or transition delays to exceed 400 milliseconds, which degrades user engagement and creates perceived sluggishness.
trigger_context: any interactive UI component responding to user input, such as button taps, form submissions, or state transitions
why: Delays exceeding 400ms disrupt the user's flow state and reduce the perceived responsiveness and quality of the software application.
example: A button tap triggers an immediate visual feedback state change and loader within 200ms, followed by network resolution.
